content:
Quick answer: For arthritis, choose walking shoes with a cushioned midsole, supportive midfoot, wide toe box and easy fastenings (Velcro, elastic laces or slip-ons). A removable insole helps if you use orthotics. Get measured late in the day when feet are largest, and ask about NHS podiatry or orthotics if foot deformity or severe pain limits walking.

The right pair will not cure arthritis, but it can make everyday walking less punishing on painful knees, hips, ankles and feet. This guide is general UK information — not a diagnosis or a product endorsement. Confirm footwear and orthotic decisions with your GP, podiatrist or physiotherapist.

What UK guidance says about movement and footwear

NICE osteoarthritis guidance (NG226) emphasises therapeutic exercise and supporting people to stay active. Shoes are not a “cure”, but better cushioning and fit can make the walking and strengthening that NICE recommends more realistic on hard UK pavements. NHS osteoarthritis pages and Versus Arthritis exercise advice likewise treat regular movement as core self-management — footwear is one practical lever that helps people keep going.

What to look for in arthritis-friendly walking shoes

  • Cushioned midsole — absorbs impact and reduces load through knees and hips
  • Arch / midfoot support — helps alignment and fatigue on longer walks
  • Wide toe box — room for bunions, toe deformity or swollen feet (see also NHS foot pain guidance)
  • Lightweight build — less effort lifting each step when joints are stiff
  • Non-slip outsole — steadier on wet pavements and kitchen floors
  • Easy fastening — Velcro, zips, pull tabs or elastic laces when hand arthritis makes tying hard
  • Removable insole — space for custom or off-the-shelf orthotics
  • Gentle rocker sole (optional) — can reduce push-off stress through stiff midfoot or big-toe joints for some walkers

Features by joint problem

Foot and ankle arthritis

Prioritise cushioning, a gentle rocker sole and a firm heel counter. Tight shoes and thin flats often aggravate midfoot and ankle pain. If deformity, ulcers or numbness are present, ask for NHS podiatry rather than guessing with fashion footwear.

Knee and hip osteoarthritis

Shock absorption matters more than fashion trainers. A modest heel-to-toe drop (about 8–12 mm) suits many walkers; completely flat, unsupportive shoes can feel harsh on concrete. Pair shoe changes with paced walking from our exercise guide and the exercise hub.

Hand arthritis

Choose closures you can manage on a bad day. If dressing is already hard, see our pain relief guide and Benefits & PIP hub for daily-living support pathways.

Fitting tips that actually help

  • Shop in the afternoon; feet swell during the day
  • Wear the socks you walk in; leave a thumb’s width at the toe
  • Try both shoes and walk on a hard floor, not only carpet
  • Check width fittings (UK wide / extra-wide) rather than sizing up blindly
  • Replace shoes when midsole cushioning feels “dead” (often 300–500 miles of walking)

Where people shop in the UK (examples, not rankings)

Comfort and wide-fit ranges commonly discussed by people with arthritis include Hotter, Cosyfeet, Skechers, New Balance and Clarks — plus high-street sports shops with gait advice. Brands change stock often; judge the features above rather than any single label. Some NHS trusts and charities also run footwear advice sessions. We do not rank products and we do not take commission in this article.

NHS footwear, podiatry and orthotics

If arthritis significantly affects your feet, your GP can refer you to NHS podiatry or orthotics. They may offer custom insoles, specialist footwear or modification advice. Bring a short note of what hurts, how far you can walk, and which shoes you already own. Versus Arthritis and NHS condition pages explain self-management alongside clinical care — start with movement guidance in our exercise guide.

Walking when newly diagnosed or in a flare

If you are newly diagnosed, start with short, frequent walks on even ground rather than long weekend miles. During a flare, shorten distance, use supportive shoes indoors if barefoot is painful, and escalate red-flag symptoms via NHS 111 or urgent care. Pair footwear changes with pacing from the arthritis pain relief guide.

Diet, weight and walking load

Even modest weight loss can reduce load through knees and feet for some people with osteoarthritis. Combine sensible walking shoes with patterns from our diet hub — Mediterranean-style eating is the usual UK evidence-aligned starting point, not miracle “joint foods”.

Money, work and getting out of the house

If pain limits how far you can walk outdoors, that can matter for Personal Independence Payment (PIP) mobility descriptors and for Access to Work adjustments (closer parking, flexible starts). Use the Benefits & PIP hub and PIP evidence diary to note real walking distances on good and bad days.

Practical next steps

  1. List what hurts now (feet, knees, hips, hands) and which shoe features you lack
  2. Book a fitting or ask your GP about podiatry if deformity or ulcers are a concern
  3. Keep a two-week note of pain (0–10) and walking distance after any shoe change
  4. Build walking into a paced plan via the exercise guide

Quick questions

Is this medical advice? No. Educational information for a UK audience — confirm choices with your NHS team.

Do expensive shoes work better? Not always. Fit, cushioning, support and fastenings matter more than price.

When should I seek urgent help? Sudden inability to bear weight, a hot swollen joint with fever, or rapidly worsening foot ulcers — use NHS 111 or A&E as appropriate.
